title: Scientists Name the 'Chunkiest' Squid Relative Ever Found
summary:
Two rare fossils from Wyoming have revealed a new kind of ancient squid relative that lived about 160 million years ago, during the Jurassic Period.

The animal has been named Wyoteuthis linsterorum. It was a belemnite, part of an extinct group of sea creatures related to today's squid and octopuses. Belemnites had a hard, bullet-shaped part inside their bodies called a rostrum. That part is often the only piece that becomes a fossil.

Belemnite fossils are very common. Wyoming's Sundance Formation, rock left behind by an ancient inland sea, has produced millions of them. Locals even nickname them squid butts. Most are narrow, about 5 to 10 centimeters long and only 1 to 2 centimeters wide.

The new species is very different. Its rostrum is about 10 centimeters long but about 6 centimeters wide, making it the thickest belemnite ever found. Scientists think the whole animal, including its arms, may have been about 60 centimeters, or two feet, long.

The first fossil was found in the late 1990s and sat in a museum drawer for years. In 2019, fossil collector Cliff Linster donated a second one to the Wyoming Dinosaur Center. With two fossils to compare, scientists could finally describe the new species.

Researchers from the United States, the United Kingdom and New Zealand used CT scans to look inside the fossils without damaging them. The scans showed it belonged to a belemnite family scientists thought had disappeared millions of years earlier.

Researcher Alexey Ippolitov suggests its large size may have helped it hunt smaller belemnites. The study was published in the journal Papers in Palaeontology.
why_it_matters: Even a fossil group studied for a very long time can still surprise scientists. The find shows an animal family survived longer than experts believed.

background_read: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of living things from long ago, often found in rock.
Belemnites were sea animals related to squid that were very common in ancient oceans, so their hard inner parts are some of the most frequently found fossils.
Millions of years ago, a shallow sea covered parts of what is now the western United States, and its rocks in Wyoming hold many sea fossils.
Scientists describe a new species by comparing specimens with known ones and publishing their findings in a science journal.
